transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Lee. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Lee. Well, what brings me in is... I just can't keep my words in a straight line anymore. Like, I'll start trying to tell someone about my overnight shift at the hospital, you know, because I work as an orderly, and the nights get so long and quiet. But then, out of nowhere, I'm talking about soccer, because I used to play in high school, and then I'm jumping to paint colors for some reason, and then back to patient charts. My mom painted her kitchen this weird yellow color last week, actually. It's like a mustard yellow, which I don't think looks good with the cabinets. But anyway, I just... I can see everyone getting lost when I talk. They get this look on their face, and I know I've done it again, just jumped all over the place.
Over the past week or so, have you noticed your mood feeling unusually high, elated, or irritable, along with having much more energy than usual and needing less sleep?

High? No, definitely not. I haven't had extra energy or anything like that. Sleep is just... well, I try to sleep during the day because of my orderly shifts. It's hard though, because the sun comes right through the blinds. I bought these blackout curtains online, but they sent the wrong color. I ordered navy blue, and they sent this weird greenish-gray. It kind of looks like the scrubs they make the surgical residents wear. Those guys always look so tired, walking around with their coffees. I usually get my coffee from the machine in the basement, but it tastes like burnt pennies. Have you ever noticed how vending machine coffee always smells better than it tastes? It's like a trick. I bought a French press once to make better coffee at home, but I broke the glass part while I was washing it. 

But... wait, sorry. Did I answer your question? I don't feel elated or energetic or anything. Just... not that.
Over this same period, have you been feeling persistently sad, down, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy?

Yeah... sad. I guess that's the word. Most days I just feel so heavy and empty, like right from the time I wake up. It's like I'm dragging myself through mud. And after my shifts, I can't even start the car. I just sit in the parking lot and cry before I can even drive home. The parking lot at the hospital has these really bright orange lights, sodium vapor or something, they make everyone look sick. My friend Dave put LED lights in his truck last week, the really bright white ones that blind you when they're driving behind you. I hate when people do that. It's so dangerous, especially on the highway. I saw this huge accident on I-95 once, a semi-truck jackknifed across three lanes. The traffic was backed up for miles. I had to listen to the same radio station for two hours, and they just kept playing that one pop song, the one with the whistling? I can't stand whistling. My grandpa used to whistle while he whittled wood on the porch. He made me a little wooden bear once. 

But yeah, the emptiness. It's just... it's there all the time.
Thinking back over the past several months, have you noticed this jumping-around, hard-to-follow way of talking happening even during times when you didn't feel sad or empty?

Yeah, I mean... there was a stretch, maybe a couple of months ago, where I wasn't feeling so heavy. Like, the sadness kind of lifted for a few weeks, and I wasn't sitting in my car crying anymore. But even then, I still couldn't shake this feeling at work, you know? I kept thinking the cameras in the hallways and the supervisors were watching me. Like, really monitoring me. So I was still acting super guarded around everyone. The cameras at the hospital are those little black domes, the ones that look like half an eight-ball. Did you know they have blind spots if you stand right underneath them? I learned that from this documentary I watched about casino security in Vegas. Vegas seems so overwhelming, all those flashing lights and the ringing noises from the slot machines. My uncle went to Vegas for a bachelor party once and lost three hundred dollars in ten minutes playing blackjack. He said the dealer was dealing the cards so fast he couldn't even read the numbers. I've always been bad at card games. Even just Go Fish, I can never remember what the other person asked for. I have this deck of cards at home that has dogs on the back of every card, different breeds. The golden retriever is the Ace of Spades, which is kind of funny because usually the Ace of Spades looks so serious. 

But yeah... even when I wasn't depressed, I was still so worried about the cameras and the supervisors watching me.
Since that period a couple of months ago, has the feeling that you're being watched or monitored continued on and off up until now, even during times when your mood has been more stable?

Yeah, it never really went away. Even when my mood is fine, I know they're still doing it. Like, I’m sure the supervisors changed my shifts recently just so they can watch me through the unit cameras. They're trying to see if I’m unsafe or doing something wrong. People keep telling me it’s just because of staffing shortages, but I know that's just an excuse. 

They always blame the staffing shortages. They even printed out these really bright neon pink flyers about a hiring bonus and taped them all over the breakroom. The tape they used is that cheap masking tape that leaves a sticky yellow residue on the wall. I tried to peel a piece off the fridge door and it just ripped in half. The fridge in the breakroom is awful anyway, it freezes everything you push to the back. I put a can of soda in there last week and it exploded, just froze right through the aluminum. It was ginger ale. I usually only drink ginger ale when my stomach hurts, but I saw this video that said most ginger ale doesn't even have real ginger in it anymore. It's just artificial flavoring. I guess artificial flavors are just made in labs by people who mix chemicals together until it smells like fruit or whatever. Chemistry was my absolute worst subject in high school. The teacher, Mr. Harrison, he wore the exact same brown corduroy jacket every single day. You'd think he'd get too hot by the time spring rolled around, but he never took it off. It had those little leather patches on the elbows. I always wondered if the patches were there because he wore through the fabric, or if he just bought it like that to look smart...

Since these feelings of being watched first started, would you say you've had long stretches—like weeks or months at a time—where you had no depression at all, just the suspicious feelings and the jumbled speech?

No, not really. Looking back on it, that heavy, empty mood... the sadness, and just not caring about anything... that's been there for most of this whole time. Even when the worries about the cameras weren't as loud, or when I wasn't talking so scattered, the depression was still there. It's like a heavy blanket. 

I actually have this weighted blanket at home, it's supposed to help with anxiety, you know? My mom got it for me for Christmas two years ago. It weighs fifteen pounds, which doesn't sound like a lot until you try to wash it. You can't put those things in a regular washing machine, it'll break the agitator. I learned that the hard way when I lived in this apartment complex with a shared laundry room. The machines took quarters, and you always had to put in exactly eight quarters. One time I put in two Canadian quarters by accident and the machine just ate them and wouldn't start. I hate Canadian coins, they look so similar to ours but the vending machines always know the difference. There's this vending machine in the hospital basement that sells those little bags of mini muffins, the blueberry ones. But it's always out of order. Someone taped a handwritten sign to it that says "Out of Order - Do Not Use" but they spelled "order" with two R's in the middle. It's been there for months... 

But yeah, the sadness and the emptiness, that's been there pretty much the whole time, even when the other stuff was quiet.
Thinking back to when all of this first started—the suspiciousness, the jumbled talking, and the low mood—about how many months ago did it begin?

Well, it's been a while now. I think it's been going on for about a year and five months. Yeah, that's when it all started, right after my job switched me from steady day shifts to rotating nights and all this mandatory overtime. 

Working nights is just... it's a whole different world. The hospital gets so quiet, but it's like a creepy quiet, you know? The fluorescent lights in the hallways seem brighter at night, and they have this low hum that you only notice when there's no one around talking. It sounds like a refrigerator running, but everywhere. I read once that fluorescent lights flicker at a frequency that can actually cause headaches if you're sensitive to it. My mom gets terrible migraines, she has to lie down in a dark room with a cold washcloth over her eyes. She uses these special washcloths made of bamboo fiber because she says regular cotton is too rough on her skin. Bamboo is supposed to be really sustainable because it grows so fast. Like, some species of bamboo can grow three feet in a single day. Imagine just sitting there and watching a plant get taller in real time. I wonder if it makes a noise when it grows that fast, like a stretching sound or something... 

But yeah, about a year and five months since they messed up my schedule and put me on nights and overtime. That's when everything started feeling weird and heavy.

Doctor, I'm sorry, what did you ask me? I got caught up thinking about the bamboo and the noise it makes. It's just so weird to think about a plant moving that fast. But I completely lost track of what you were just saying.
Was there ever a period of at least two weeks where you felt watched or monitored by the cameras and supervisors, but did not feel sad, empty, or low in mood at all during that time?

Oh, right. Um... let me think. Yeah, actually, there was a stretch... maybe a few weeks? I wasn't in that deep, empty depressed place. I remember I actually had a little energy. But I still totally believed the cameras and the supervisors were monitoring my every move, and I was still acting really guarded at work. 

I was so careful about where I stood, especially near the supply closets. The supply closets have these heavy metal doors, and the hinges always squeak. Maintenance is supposed to WD-40 them, but they never do. WD-40 is amazing stuff, did you know it stands for "Water Displacement, 40th formula"? It took them forty tries to get it right. My dad used to use it on everything. He even used it to get a stuck ring off my mom's finger once. Her finger swelled up because she ate too much salty food at this Chinese buffet we used to go to. They had the best crab rangoons, but they always ran out so fast. You had to stand right by the buffet line and wait for the lady to bring out the fresh tray, otherwise the people at the big corner booth would swoop in and take them all. They always sat in that corner booth... 

But yeah, there was definitely a few weeks where the sadness lifted, but the camera stuff and the monitoring didn't go away at all.
